title: Tongues, Love, and Perfect Knowledge
english: Those [gifts] are given to the unworthy for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love belongs to the pious man. Therefore he says: lay hold of the better gifts. And I show you a way that leads you to the enjoyment of the superior gifts, namely the way of love; for the one loving fulfills the law. And the one fulfilling the law is well-pleasing. And the one being well-pleasing receives a spiritual gift.

Because he saw them desiring those who possess the gifts, but not warming the love, he teaches that love is the most supreme good; for those gifts are such that even to the unworthy they were given for the building up of the church, but the achievement of love is the own property of the pious man. So he says the way of love leads us to the enjoyment of the superior [gifts]; for what is higher than the gift of love which fulfills all the law?

And what tongue of angels, with whom there is no chest, no larynx, no tongue, no voice? But rather, as Moses says in Deuteronomy, God set limits of nations according to the number of the angels of God—and clearly He set them when He divided into tongues those attempting to build the tower—because they no longer guarded a common concord but, as if they were made strangers to one another by the changes of language, angels were set, so that each might guard the nation to which he was entrusted, and nothing might be consumed or perish. Because of this, he calls the difference of languages the tongues of angels.

And it must be known that just as David says 'bread of angels' not as something for eating, so also 'tongues of angels' is not for speaking; for this too is as ministering to the decree of God. Human language is that which is trained—for this is acquired, unlike the natural kind—but the language of angels is that which is divided into many by nature. I have become a sounding bronze or a clanging cymbal.

From here it appears that he calls the alternation and difference of languages the tongues of angels; for the one speaking in other tongues to those who do not know them is like a cymbal producing only a sound, without any meaning being shown. He calls human language rhetorical, grammatical, philosophical, intellectual, compositional, technical, and dialectical. But what tongue is it among angels, with whom there is no chest, no larynx, no voice, nor anything else bodily?

Regarding the tongues, he speaks of the differences of languages which the angels established according to the dispersion at the tower, so that each might guard what was entrusted to a nation. Just as we understand a bread of angels to be that which is provided through the command of the angels—not that the angels were eating, but that the angels were commanded to provide—so also the tongues of angels are the differences of languages which angels established. He spoke of the differences of languages as the clanging of a bronze trumpet and a cymbal; for when someone does not know what is being spoken in another language, the speaker is to him like a meaningless cymbal, and the meaning is not made manifest.

Everything that is unknown is called a mystery, but it is revealed by the power of the Spirit. This is one mystery, as he says elsewhere: 'For I do not want you to be ignorant of this mystery,' and again, 'Behold, I say a mystery to us.' After a little while he teaches what love is, where he says: 'Love is patient' and the following. Therefore, to show mercy is one thing and to love is another, yet even to give one's substance to the poor and to give oneself up for martyrdom—if this happens through word alone regarding love, it falls into vanity and empty ambition. Therefore, whether we give because of love for the receiver, or because we are giving on behalf of the God who commanded, and whether we bear witness because of love for the Lord, this we must endure. Love never fails, that is, it never slips into sin. The partial is done away when the whole knowledge is given; for we know but a little of the many things still hidden.

As he says, when I was a child, I had the thoughts of an infant, but having passed into a mature man, I have the mind; no longer merely knowing the father as father, but also what kind of father he is. In the same way, that I know now in part, this I shall learn in the perfect time. And what now is as if in a dim mirror, this I shall know clearly in the time. He did not say 'I will know the mysteries then,' which would follow, but 'I shall be known'; for the one who is known by God and made His own, such a one attains the direct sight of the mysteries. Lest all knowledge being revealed to us, there remains to us the believing that all knowledge shall be revealed to us.
translator_notes: True OET; Pass A ≠ Pass B. Melito skipped; never Cyril Matthew densify.
baehrens: PG Fragmenta in epistulam i ad Corinthios u05-rem-early

title: The distinction between tongues and prophecy
english: They believe in order to hope, but necessary love is to hope so that we do not fall from hope. Therefore he said: love is greater than this; for through love the law is fulfilled.

For if one does not interpret, but only speaks in a tongue and does not manifest the power, as one not possessing this gift of interpretation, he speaks mysteries indeed—for the Spirit provides tongues—and he utters mysteries through the tongues, but he does not build up the church, not understanding what he says. He who speaks in a tongue builds himself up, knowing that what he did not already utter was intelligible; it was a grace of the Holy Spirit in him and he was building up. Just as one speaking in tongues and interpreting is not less than the prophet. Zeal for the prophecy more than the other gifts, he says. And this he said: for to each according to his administration the gifts were given, and in them was what he wished to zealously seek and receive.

But when some speak in tongues, no listener understands. However, even if the things spoken are indistinct to men, the one speaking in the spirit speaks mysteries—for the Spirit provides mysteries through tongues—the one prophesying benefits those who hear, for he speaks clearly to them. The grace is greater if the one speaking in tongues also receives to interpret; for perhaps he did not obtain both. Just as one speaking in tongues and interpreting is not less than the prophet.

What will I benefit you, he says, if I am not able to speak to you either about what was revealed to me by God, or about what he himself knew and understood, or about what he understood through prophets, or about what he knew to advise or teach you? If I speak about these things and you do not understand, what will I benefit you? Observe, for he says, that even in the pipes and lyre, if the sounds are not distinguished, the piping or the lyre-playing is blended together. Nothing is without sound, clearly, a kind of human. He speaks the various gifts of the Holy Spirit spiritually.

If, he says, I speak in a tongue which I do not know, not even knowing its power, I am convinced that I have an unfruitful mind, not having the power of the things said. Let him pray so that he may obtain a double grace, to speak in tongues and to interpret these.

To be a tongue is an operation of the Holy Spirit, but for the mind it becomes fruitlessness because of the inability to understand or be benefited by what is being said. Therefore, he says, this must be done by me: to make clear what is supplied to me through the Spirit for the building up of those hearing, so that the mind is not fruitless by lacking the power of the words. Because if I give thanks with a tongue but no one can understand or benefit from what is said, the listener does not give the 'Amen'. He calls the 'layman' like a soldier who has not yet been baptized. He speaks of clarity of mind and common language. Strive to be perfect, to understand the Scriptures.

It must be noted that the Jews, being required, where God spoke to them in many tongues, they were disobedient and have nothing to show; but we demonstrate that when the Holy Spirit came and distributed tongues, the disobedient Jews were saying, 'They are drunk on sweet wine.' Thus, tongues are a sign not for the believers but for the unbelievers, and prophecy is not for the unbelievers but for the believers. Thus, tongues build up when the hearer learns that the speaker speaks a tongue he did not know; yet he does not receive the building up of the benefit of spiritual teaching because of the lack of understanding, so that no progress is made. For prophecy is for those coming, but regarding these things, the one who happens to be there is not the unbeliever but the faithful one.

The unbeliever has need of the one not knowing the tongue used, and of the one demonstrating that it is the Spirit of God in him. Thus, the tongue was a wonder, but prophecy is a wonder from its outcome, not in the speaking itself. Unbelief is said in two ways in the Divine Scripture: the true unbelief is that of the Greeks, and the little faith is that of the pious. He calls the Greek 'unbelieving', and the 'layman' the soldier who has not yet been baptized; for then they did not say 'catechumens' or 'unbaptized'. He calls them 'Law-abiding' like the other prophets, because they lived according to the Law. What was said to Isaiah then applied when the Spirit descended upon the apostles, and they spoke in tongues and the Jews mocked. It is clear that tongues benefit when the hearer knows that the speaker speaks a tongue he did not know nor learned from men; nevertheless, the matter does not benefit the...

title: The Necessity of the Resurrection
english: The listener is called an auditor because he does not perceive. Prophecy is given to the faithful, speaking of things to come, to those who do not believe by chance but who are faithful. The sign is given to the unbelieving so that he may believe what he sees, but prophecy is given so that he may confirm what is said and bless the Lord. The Greek is called an unbeliever, and the one being catechized is called a fool; and there are places where even the little-believing is called an unbeliever.

Each one, through which grace he has from God, let him build up the church by this. Having said this, he taught that one speaks by the Holy Spirit when he wishes to speak and is silent just as the prophets, not indeed those restrained by an unclean spirit; for they, even when they do not wish to speak, speak things they do not know. Through these things he shows that the Holy Spirit revealed mysteries to the souls, and that to be enlightened there, it was revealed to men, not like in the divinations where the diviner does not know what he utters. Therefore he gave back that first thing which he was saying, that when you were Gentiles toward the mute idols, as you were being led away.

Let two or three prophets speak, and let the others discern, those having the gift of the discerning of spirits. If to another it is revealed while sitting, let the first be silent, as it is in them sometimes to be silent and sometimes to speak. And the spirits of prophets are subject to prophets. Do not fear, he says, if you keep silent as if rejecting the Spirit; for he knows that the gifts are to be subject to one another. It is manifest that those having the gifts of the discerning of spirits [should use them], so that the church may receive building up and not trouble from all speaking at once.

I say not something foreign, he says, but what I preached. And not only did I preach, but you did not receive, but what also you received. And you did not receive in vain or without foundation, but in which you are being saved. He says that he is about to say that he made known to you that the Lord Jesus died for us; by what word is this gospel, so that the resurrection may be believed; for Jesus is the firstfruits of the resurrection, having died for us. For if death were not to be abolished, the Savior would not have become man, unless in vain he returned.

You received it, instead of 'except that you believed in vain'; for I say that if you do not hold fast, it is evident that you believed in vain. The word of the gospel is the resurrection from the dead, the beginning of which is Christ. For if God did not intend for death to be taken away, He would not have become human. Therefore, if you do not hold fast to what you heard but have rejected it, it is clear that you believed in vain. The term 'instead of' stands for 'but'.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:3, 'In the first place' means 'before all things'; I delivered this to you. 'In the first place' means 'before all things'. I did not deliver a mere argument of my own, but what I received from the Scriptures. It was confirmed by eyewitnesses, that Christ, having died, rose and called him from heaven. Regarding 1 Cor 15:4, how was He buried, if He did not have flesh, according to the heretics? Regarding 1 Cor 15:6, 'instead of' means 'more than'.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:8, an abortion is that which is cast out in the womb before being formed and receiving the time due to it, which also cannot live. Just as in the womb infants are being formed, so in the Law souls were being pre-formed toward piety, and were born of water and Spirit. But Paul persecuted the church without being formed in the Law toward perfection—for he did persecute—therefore he called himself an abortion, and he brings this forth further: because I persecuted the church of God. Infants cast out before being formed in the womb are called abortions. Since in the Law souls were being pre-formed toward piety and were born of water and Spirit, but Paul, as one not having been formed in the Law, persecuted the church, therefore he rightly names himself an abortion.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:9–10a, 'least among the apostles', since he did not persecute them but, having believed, he persecuted. Being a persecutor, he happened to receive such grace according to the foreknowledge of God, so that he labored more than the others. Regarding 1 Cor 15:10b, 'not in vain did I receive much grace', but I used it for the sake of the preaching, laboring more than all of them. 'Instead of' means 'not in vain did I receive the grace'; for I have labored.

Regarding 1 Cor 15:12–13, it is not possible that Christ rose and the rest do not; but, to speak in agreement, if for nothing Christ died and rose, then through nothing is our resurrection. Regarding 1 Cor 15:14–18, he says, if Christ has not been raised, then in vain.
